## Instructions

For each problem, please write a complete argument, not only intermediate calculations. Answers without justification may receive zero credit. Collaboration is encouraged, but you must write your own final solutions independently.

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">1</span> **Primes and Fermat numbers.** For $n\ge0$, the $n$th *Fermat number* is defined by
$F_n=2^{2^n}+1$.

(1\) Prove by induction that $F_0F_1\cdots F_{n-1}=F_n-2$ for every $n\ge1$.

(2\) Deduce from part (1) that any two distinct Fermat numbers are relatively prime.

(3\) Based on part (2), give another proof that there are infinitely many primes.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">2</span> **Primes modulo 8.** We proved in class that there are infinitely many primes
$p\equiv 5\pmod 8$. The goal of this problem is to show that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$
and that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv 7\pmod 8$, while leaving the remaining case $p\equiv 1\pmod 8$ to the next problem.

(1\) Let $a\in\mathbb Z$. Show that every odd prime $p\mid a^2-2$ satisfies $p\equiv 1\text{ or }7\pmod8$.

(2\) Use part (1) to prove that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv 7\pmod 8$.

(3\) Describe how the proof can be modified to show that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$.

</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">3</span> **Primes $\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$.** Let $n\ge1$ be an integer. We show that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$.

(1\) Euler's theorem asserts that given any integers $a\in\mathbb Z$ and $m\ge1$ with $\gcd(a,m)=1$, we have
$$a^{\phi(m)}\equiv 1\pmod m.$$ The *order of* $a$ *modulo* $m$, denoted by $\text{ord}_m(a)$, is
the least positive integer $d$ such that $a^d\equiv 1\pmod m$. Thus, Euler's theorem implies that $\text{ord}_m(a)$
exists and satisfies $1\le\text{ord}_m(a)\le\phi(m)$. Prove that if $k$ is any positive integer such that
$a^k\equiv1\pmod m$, then $\text{ord}_m(a)\mid k$.
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Use the division algorithm.
</details>

(2\) Deduce from part (1) that if $p$ is an odd prime dividing $a^{2^{n-1}}+1$ for some $a\in\mathbb Z$, then
$\text{ord}_p(a)=2^n$ and $p\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$.

(3\) Use part (2) to show that there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$.

</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">4</span> **Primes and quadratic residues.** Suppose that $a\in\mathbb Z$ is not a perfect square. We show that there are infinitely many odd primes $p$ such that
$a\text{ R }p$ and that there are infinitely many odd primes $p$ such that
$a\text{ N }p$. Note that the case when $a$ has no odd prime factor $q$ with $2\nmid e_q(a)$ boils down to $\pm2\pmod p$. This case follows from the infinitude of primes in residue classes modulo 8 that we have fully resolved. In parts (b) and (c) below, we are therefore allowed to assume that $a$ has an odd prime factor $q$ with $2\nmid e_q(a)$. In these two parts, we will also use the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT), which states that
if $m_1,\ldots,m_k\ge1$ are pairwise relatively prime,
namely $\gcd(m_i,m_j)=1$ for all $1\le i<j\le k$,
and if $a_1,\ldots,a_k\in\mathbb Z$ are arbitrary,
then the system of linear congruences
$$
\left\{
\begin{alignedat}{2}
x &\equiv a_1 && \pmod{m_1}\\
x &\equiv a_2 && \pmod{m_2}\\
&\ \ \vdots && \qquad\vdots\\
x &\equiv a_k && \pmod{m_k}
\end{alignedat}
\right.
$$
has a unique solution $x$ modulo $M=m_1\cdots m_k$. In particular, it has a unique solution $0\le x<M$.

(1\) Use numbers of the form $x^2-a$ to show that there are infinitely many odd primes $p$ such that
$a\text{ R }p$.
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Consider the number $n=((|a|+3)p_1\cdots p_k)^2-a$, where $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ are odd primes such that $a\text{ R }p_i$ for every $1\le i\le k$.
</details>


(2\) Suppose that $a$ has an odd prime factor $q$ with $2\nmid e_q(a)$. We may write $a=\varepsilon 2^u q^{2v+1}b^2c$,
where $\varepsilon=\pm1$, $u,v\ge0$, $b\ge1$ with $q\nmid b$, and $c\ge1$ is squarefree and odd with $q\nmid c$.
Let $h$ be a quadratic nonresidue modulo $q$ and let $m\ge1$ be an integer with $\gcd(m,q)=1$.
Since $\gcd(q,8bcm)=1$, CRT implies that
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
x&\equiv h\pmod q\\
x&\equiv 1\pmod{8bcm}
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$
has a unique solution $0\le x<8bcmq$. Note that $\gcd(x,2am)=1$. Let $n=x+8bcmq>1$. Use the properties of the Jacobi symbol from
Problem 7 of Homework 2 to prove
$$
\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)=-1.
$$

(3\) As in part (2), suppose that $a$ has an odd prime factor $q$ with $2\nmid e_q(a)$. Assume that there were only finitely many odd primes
$p_1,\ldots,p_k$ such that $a\text{ N }p_i$, where $1\le i\le k$. Take $m=p_1\cdots p_k\ge1$. Then $\gcd(m,q)=1$. Part (2) produces an odd integer $n>1$
such that $n\equiv1\pmod m$ and
$$
\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)=-1.
$$
Show that $n$ has a prime factor $p\ne p_1,\ldots,p_k$ satisfying $a\text{ N }p$ and conclude by contradiction that there are infinitely many
odd primes $p$ such that $a\text{ N }p$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">5</span> **Parity of the divisor functions.** Recall that $\tau(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}1$ and
$\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d$ count the positive divisors and sum the positive divisors of $n$,respectively.

(1\) Prove that $\tau(n)$ is odd if and only if $n$ is a perfect square.

(2\) Prove that $\sigma(n)$ is odd if and only if $n$ is a perfect square or twice a perfect square.

</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">6</span> **A sum of greatest common divisors.** For a positive integer $n$, define
$$
G(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n).
$$
(1\) Prove that
$$
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\phi\left(\frac nd\right).
$$
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Group the integers $1\le k\le n$ according to the value of $\gcd(k,n)$.
</details>

(2\) Deduce that $G$ is multiplicative and that if $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$ is its prime
factorization, then
$$
G(n)=n\prod_{i=1}^{r}
\left(1+a_i\left(1-\frac1{p_i}\right)\right).
$$

(3\) Compute $G(360)$ using the formula from part (2).

</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">7</span> **Detecting squares with the Liouville function.** Let $\lambda(n)=(-1)^{\Omega(n)}$ be the
*Liouville function*, where $\Omega(n)=\sum_{p}e_p(n)$. Then $\lambda(n)$ is completely multiplicative.

(1\) Prove that
$$
\sum_{d\mid n}\lambda(d)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if $n$ is a perfect square},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

(2\) Use Möbius inversion and part (1) to prove that
$$
\lambda(n)=
\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu\left(\frac{n}{d^2}\right).
$$
</div>



## Optional challenge

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">8</span> **The $\boldsymbol{n}$th prime.** Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime. For instance, $p_1=2$, $p_2=3$, $p_3=5$, $p_4=7$, and so on. As usual, let $\pi(N)$
denote the number of primes not exceeding $N$. Then $\pi(p_n)=n$ and $p_{\pi(N)}=N$.

(1\) Suppose that there are constants $0<A<B$ and an integer $N_0\ge53$ such that
   $$A\frac{N}{\ln N}<\pi(N)<B\frac{N}{\ln N},\qquad N\ge N_0.$$
Show that 
   $$\frac{1}{B}n\ln n<p_n<\frac{e^{f(n)}}{A}n\ln n\qquad n\ge \pi(N_0),$$
where
$$f(n)=-\ln A\cdot\frac{\ln(\ln n)}{\ln n}+2\ln\frac{n}{A}\cdot\left(\frac{\ln(\ln n)}{\ln n}\right)^2.$$
The assumption $N_0\ge53$ ensures that $\pi(N_0)\ge\pi(53)=16$. You may use without proof the inequality
$$\frac{1}{1-x}<1+x+2x^{2},\qquad x\in(0,1/2),$$	
and the fact that 
\[g(x)=\frac{\ln(\ln x)}{\ln x}\]
is strictly decreasing on $[16,\infty)$ and attains global maximum $g(16)<1/2$.
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Note that $p_n>n$. To prove the upper bound, take $\ln$ to get
$$A(1-g(p_n))\ln p_n=A(\ln p_n-\ln(\ln p_n))<\ln\pi(p_n)=\ln n.$$
</details>

(2\) Suppose that there are constants $0<C<D$ and an integer $N_0\ge\max\{2,D^2\}$ such that
$$Cn\ln n<p_n<Dn\ln n,\qquad n\ge \pi(N_0).$$
Prove that
$$\frac{1}{D}\cdot\frac{N}{\ln N}<\pi(N)<\frac{1}{C}\cdot\frac{N}{\ln N-\ln(\ln N)-\ln D},\qquad N\ge N_0.$$
(The assumption $N_0\ge\max\{2,D^2\}$ ensures that $N_0\ge2$ and $\ln N-\ln(\ln N)-\ln D>0$ for all $N\ge N_0$.)

(3\) Recall that the Prime Number Theorem (PNT) states that
$$\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}\frac{\pi(N)}{N/\ln N}=1.$$
Use parts (a) and (b) to prove that PNT is equivalent to
$$\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_n}{n\ln n}=1.$$
<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Use the $\varepsilon$-$N$ definition of limit.
</details>
</div>

</div>
